query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small controlled amount of nanoprecipitate‐promoting alloying elements (e.g., Nb or Ti) to the CoCrFeNi matrix will enable in situ formation of a nanohierarchical microstructure that yields adaptive friction interface protection at room temperature and rapid formation of a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer at high temperature, thereby reducing both the friction coefficient and wear rate consistently from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with an fcc structure.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying addition (e.g., Nb or Ti) designed to trigger nanoprecipitate formation during processing/annealing.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests performed from room temperature (≈25 °C) to 800 °C, under a load of ~5 N with sliding conditions similar to those in a linear reciprocating friction test in ambient or mildly oxidative environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanohierarchical microstructure comprising nano-coupled grains and uniformly distributed nanoprecipitates that can evolve into a protective, dense nanocrystalline glaze layer at elevated temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, the nanoprecipitates lead to a gradient frictional stress release through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways. At high temperature, the same nanoprecipitates aid in the development of a nanocrystalline glaze layer that minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear, thereby maintaining a low friction coefficient. This dual-purpose mechanism allows protection across the full temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the starting CoCrFeNi alloy, the modified alloy with nanoprecipitates is predicted to exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction and wear rate under sliding with performance improvements sustained across the full temperature range tested (room temperature to 800 °C).
generation.baseline: Original CoCrFeNi alloy without nanoprecipitate-promoting additions, which suffers from increased friction and wear rate especially at the high-temperature end of the test range.
generation.boundary: Temperature: 25 °C to 800 °C; Load: ~5 N; Environment: conditions similar to ambient air or mildly oxidative electrolytic settings as used in reciprocating tests.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and processing window required to reliably induce the desired nano-structural features and glaze formation across such a wide temperature range remains to be optimized. The quantitative magnitude of the improvements in friction coefficient and wear rates is also uncertain until experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and another set modified with a controlled minor addition of Nb (or Ti) expected to promote nanoprecipitate formation. Process both sets under identical heat-treatment conditions to allow for potential nano feature development. Subject the samples to reciprocating sliding tests under identical conditions (load ~5 N, sliding frequency 1 Hz, test duration 30 minutes) at various temperatures spanning from room temperature to 800 °C.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) recorded in real time during sliding
Wear volume/wear rate measurements post-test using profilometry or equivalent methods
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to verify the formation of nanoprecipitates and the existence of a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in both COF and wear rate compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy across the temperature range, or if microstructural analysis fails to demonstrate the formation of the targeted nanohierarchical and glazing microstructures, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.
